The citizens commute between home, the office, and, most importantly, the pub. Your task as a player is to develop a bus line which takes as many passengers as possible to the place they want to be. You do this by expanding your bus line, developing new suburbs, luring new potential passengers to the city, and investing in more and more buses! But you can also try to run your buses just a bit earlier than other companies and steal their passengers away. Sometimes, something unexpected happens: Time comes to a standstill and, all of a sudden, the demand for transportation is completely different. But you cannot let this happen too often, as the space-time continuum will rupture and the universe will collapse, thus ending the game. [Rating: 1/10] Winner is first player at 10 tables. Easy hate drafting game. Tokens are slippery and too small for $90.

[Rating: 1/10] It's cute and chaotic, but I suspect the action-selection board is more meant to reward careful planners than punish them. I kind of enjoy how that's mixed with chaos, but can also see where it would get agonizing and long. In practice, I wonder why there's so few passenger pieces compared to the length of the game, and I suspect that's the bit meant to reward careful planners, they can foresee everything after a certain point. [Rating: 2/10] Must have been a novelty when first released but by today's standards it's well below the average. Slow and fiddly with a killer downtime between turns. The gameplay is basically about building the game board which feels weird and so very dated. In the world of modern, cutthroat worker placement games there is no excuse to play this apart from nostalgia values. Compared to Bus, Puerto Rico feels fresh off the boat (pun intended).

[Rating: 2/10] This game is awful.   It does have some interesting mechanisms, but having only one (hotly contested) possible way of scoring points (the Vrooom action) means that the eventual winner might be in doubt, but a player that's fallen behind is definitely out of the running with multiple turns remaining. This means that the player is forced to play more turns, and will merely be kingmaking with his decisions. [Rating: 2/10] Not sure why this game gets such a high rating. It quite dull to play. It does not feel like it will get any better with more plays.

[Rating: 2/10] Had a really rough time with one. I like that the setup is rather quick and the ruleset is limited (not straightforward, unfortunately), but that's about it. Visually it's just unappealing, and the quality of the game pieces is not even mediocre these days. The worst part is how this game stretches out - especially in a more competitive environment.   The game has no hidden information and no randomness, so it is technically possible to predict all of the outcomes of your and your opponents' decisions. [Rating: 2/10] Ugh! What a miserable play experience. It's not actually that it's a bad design. But it's apparently designed with the goal to deliver a bad experience.  I think, I'm finally cured of wanting to try any more 'Splotter games'.

[Rating: 2/10] Easy to learn and play. Too mean of a game, core gameplay is block the other players, zero fun when you’re blocked the entire game with no way out.

[Rating: 2.82/10] Sooooo boring. Played once. No need to play again. Not a game that needed to be remade. Buyer beware

[Rating: 3/10] We ground this game into dirt because people kept paying to prevent the clock from advancing.  Do the players who like the game routinely pay to make sure the clock does advance, I wonder?

[Rating: 3/10] Is it over yet? Dry = no luck, full information, very mechanical and tactical gameplay. Bus was probably a better game years ago when there weren't that many worker placement games around. Now there is no shortage of those and Bus shows its age in a bad way.

[Rating: 3/10] The Clock is really a stupid design.The machine that stop the time also stops me from play it more.

[Rating: 3/10] Not at all a fan of the planning and resolution system (as also seen in Dominant Species).  I don't like games that are plan, plan, plan, plan, plan, resolve.  As all of these plans will be subject to player chaos (some that is possible to predict and others not so much).  I much prefer worker placement games that let you resolve actions immediately.  Caylus being the only exception (but in Caylus other player's worker actions won't impact you to such a large degree as those in Bus and Dominant Species do).
